questions.question: How does Chesterton's essay encourage readers to approach life? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Chesterton encourages readers to adopt an attitude of cheerful acceptance and imaginative
  • reframing toward life's inconveniences - argues that right mental attitude can transform
  • ordinary mishaps into worthwhile adventures - criticizes modern pessimist tendencies - with
  • the aid of paradox and wit elucidates how the same event can be either a nuisance or an
  • excitement depending solely on perception - ncourages readers to reframe misfortune as
  • opportunity for engagement and embrace wonder at everyday experience. [A]/[CO1]

questions.question: Discuss Francis Bacon’s contribution to the essay form in English literature. How are his essays characterized? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Francis Bacon - father of the English essay - introduced essay form to English literature –
  • adapted Montaigne's French model, known for its brevity and compression. Uses quotable
  • maxims ideal for memorization - detached and prescriptive - concerned with universal
  • human behavior rather than personal confession - focus on navigating public and private life
  • successfully - applies scientific empirical observation to human affairs - elevated the essay
  • from a personal literary exercise to a serious instrument of moral and intellectual inquiry.
  • [U]/[CO1]

questions.question: What does Higgins bet Pickering regarding Eliza? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Act 2 of Shaw's Pygmalion - Professor Higgins wagers with Colonel Pickering that he can
  • transform Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl with coarse speech into someone who can
  • pass as a duchess at an ambassador's garden party within six months - Higgins boasts that
  • through phonetic training alone, he can remake Eliza's speech - The bet is ultimately the
  • engine of the play's moral argument: by treating Eliza as an object of experiment, it exposes
  • class as mere performance.
  • [K]/[CO2]

questions.question: Role of language in exploring social mobility and prejudice / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Language is the primary marker of social class and identity - Shaw uses Eliza's
  • transformation from Cockney-speaking flower girl to seemingly refined lady to expose the
  • arbitrariness of class distinctions - Through her transformation Shaw demonstrates that class
  • is performative rather than essential - Higgins’ view of Eliza's original speech as a moral as
  • well as phonetic failing reflects wider social prejudice that associated linguistic difference
  • with inferiority. [U]/[CO2]

questions.question: Discuss the class-specific nature of classical tragedy and comedy. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Tragedy traditionally features characters of noble birth—whose downfall evokes pity and
  • fear. Their elevated status makes their fall more profound and tragic. In contrast, comedy
  • usually deals with characters from lower or middle classes, focusing on ordinary life and
  • relatable flaws. CO2

questions.question: Describe the three unities derived from Aristotle's Poetics. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• The Three Unities - dramatic principles derived from Aristotle's Poetics: (i) Unity of Action
  • – double provision – plot should be either purely tragic or purely comic, but not a mixture of
  • the two (ii) Unity of Time – time over which the plot is spread should be the same or
  • approximately the same as the time of staging the play (iii) Unity of Place – a natural
  • corollary to the unity of time – as the play stages events of few hours, it should be limited to
  • one place [U]/[CO2]

questions.question: Analyse the use of music in The Great Dictator. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Music functions as satire, emotional counterpoint, and political commentary - most iconic
  • musical moment is Hynkel's ballet - megalomaniacal fantasies of world domination
  • juxtaposed with delicate, yearning music producing a satirical irony - the music in the
  • background of the Jewish Barber and his dance humanizes the Barber - overall score uses
  • military brass and march rhythms for the Tomainian scenes to parody fascist pomp, while
  • warmer, more lyrical themes accompany the Ghetto scenes - lack of musical underscore in
  • Chaplin’s famous closing speech is also critical, improving its emotional weight.
  • [An]/[CO3]

  • of costume as storytelling - Eliza's opening wardrobe - layers of mismatched and drab
  • clothing is a representation of her poverty and social marginalization - Eliza’s exquisite
  • black-and-white striped gown paired with a dramatic hat and the white gown for the
  • ambassador's ball are visual representations of her class mobility - costumes in the final
  • scenes reflect Eliza's ambiguous position of being outwardly refined but internally conflicted
  • - Beaton's designs track not just social status but emotional and psychological states of the
  • character throughout the film.

questions.question: Examine the initial encounter between Eliza Doolittle and Henry Higgins in My Fair Lady. How does this scene introduce their contrasting personalities and foreshadow the dynamics of their relationship throughout the film? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Eliza Doolittle is a young Cockney woman who is selling flowers in Covent Garden on a
  • rainy evening. When Higgins, a phonetics professor overhears Eliza speaking, starts making
  • notes, and in a somewhat condescending manner, he remarks on her rough accent, as though
  • she is a linguistic specimen to be studied. He sees her less as a person and more as an object
  • to be transformed. He brags that Eliza’s accent is the only reason she is poor, and he could
  • pass her off as nobility after six months of speech lessons. The opening scene in the film
  • foreshadows the conflict and dynamics that will unfold: Higgins’ belief in his superiority
  • and his desire to control the transformation, contrasted with Eliza's growing sense of
  • independence and self-worth. CO4

questions.question: Discuss the significance of Eliza's transformation in My Fair Lady and how the final scene reflects the challenges of navigating social mobility and personal identity. Does the ending reinforce or undermine Eliza's newfound independence? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• My Fair Lady (1964) centres on Eliza Doolittle's transformation from Cockney flower girl to
  • apparent society lady, a journey that exposes class as performative rather than natural. At the
  • Embassy Ball, she passes as a duchess, yet the transformation is fundamentally ambiguous:
  • Higgins trains her voice, but her intelligence and dignity were always her own. As Eliza
  • insists, it was Pickering's respectful treatment, not Higgins's lessons, that truly shaped her.
  • However, this mobility comes at a cost. Eliza belongs fully to neither world. She is too
  • refined for Covent Garden, yet still an outsider in the upper class. Her access remains
  • conditional, dependent on male patronage and the exhausting performance of a borrowed
  • identity. The ending undermines her independence: despite her confrontation ("I can do
  • without you"), Eliza returns to a man who never apologized and whose final request for his
  • slippers reinstates domestic hierarchy — surrendering Shaw's feminist vision to romantic
  • convention. [U]/[CO4]

questions.question: Analyze the differences between formal and informal essays, providing examples from notable essayists like Francis Bacon and Charles Lamb. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Formal Essays- an impersonal and objective composition, usually used for the discussion of
  • ideas or knowledge - introduced to England by Francis Bacon - who wrote in short,
  • crisp sentences that read like aphorisms about "counsels, civil and moral”. Informal Essays –

questions.question: Discuss the significance of dramatic structure (Exposition, Rising Action, Climax, Falling Action, and Denouement) in the development of a play, referring to B. Prasad's views. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Since Aristotle's Poetics, dramatic structure has been central to literary theory. B. Prasad, in
  • A Background to the Study of English Literature , presents the five-stage model comprising
  • Exposition, Rising Action, Climax, Falling Action, and Denouement. The exposition
  • establishes setting, characters, and conflict, but must engage the audience immediately rather
  • than merely deliver information. The rising action, the longest stage, builds complications
  • with causal coherence with each event growing inevitably from the last while revealing
  • character under pressure. The climax is the turning point where tension peaks; it must be
  • earned through preparation to achieve genuine dramatic force rather than mere sensation.
  • The falling action works out consequences at a carefully managed pace, while the
  • denouement resolves all narrative threads. Crucially, Prasad argues that great drama uses
  • this final stage to crystallize the theme — transforming the ending into philosophical
  • revelation rather than simple conclusion.
  • [An]/[CO1]

questions.question: Compare the use of space in classical Greek, Elizabethan, and modern theater. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Classical Theatre: Greek theatre was performed in large open-air amphitheatres with tiered
  • seating and a circular orchestra. Space was symbolic and ritualistic, used for processions and
  • choral movements. The structure ensured visibility, audibility, and communal viewing.
  • Elizabethan Theatre: Theatres like The Globe had thrust stages projecting into the audience,
  • creating intimacy. They were open-roofed, with galleries and the pit reflecting social
  • divisions. There were no elaborate sets—space was used suggestively, relying on language
  • and actor movement. Modern Theatre: It uses diverse spaces: proscenium, thrust, black box,
  • and theatre-in-the-round. Realism demands detailed sets; symbolic and abstract staging is
  • also common. Technology allows flexible lighting, projections, and sound to redefine spatial
  • experience. CO2

questions.question: Explain how the process of writing a drama differs significantly from that of writing a novel. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Drama and the novel both explore character and conflict, but their compositional demands
  • differ fundamentally. Unlike a dramatist, a novelist enjoys almost unlimited freedom
  • enabling a narrator to describe settings, reveal inner thoughts, and move freely across time
  • and place.The most significant difference is the absence of a narrative voice. Everything the
  • audience learns must emerge through dialogue and visible action alone, thus the novelist can
  • afford exploratory dialogue; the playwright cannot waste a single exchange.Drama imposes
  • strict spatial, temporal, and practical constraints, forcing the dramatist toward economy and
  • structural precision. Finally, unlike the novel, a fixed, complete text, a play is always a
  • blueprint for performance producing a different experience every time.
  • [U]/[CO2]

questions.question: Critically examine Chaplin’s performance as the Jewish Barber and Hynkel. / [CO3] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Chaplin's double role in The Great Dictator is the film's philosophical core. As the Jewish
  • Barber, heir to his "Little Tramp" persona, Chaplin embodies gentleness, physical grace, and
  • instinctive decency. As Hynkel, he delivers a contrasting performance of operatic excess: his
  • mock-German speeches strip fascist rhetoric of content to expose it as pure theatrical
  • manipulation, while the globe scene reveals the tyrant as a narcissistic child rather than a
  • figure of genuine authority. The double role carries a deeper philosophical argument:
  • persecutor and persecuted are physically identical, insisting that no racial hierarchy has any
  • natural basis. This culminates in the Barber's closing speech, where the victim takes the
  • oppressor's place to speak for human dignity. Though Ebert notes the film softens Nazi
  • violence and the final speech risks breaking the satirical spell, Chaplin's dual performance
  • remains proof that comedy can be one of political art's most powerful instruments.
  • [An]/[CO3]
